n101.text: Last time, we learnt that a freely suspended magnet comes to rest in the North-South direction, every time. That is because Earth behaves like a magnet.

n202.text: A little sea turtle is hiding in this video. Can you spot it?

n203b.text: Turtles pop up to breathe. Watch the water!

n204.text: Lock in first with your fingers. One finger for every point.

n401.text: Round one. Basil brings his bar magnet close to Momo's compass. What happens? One, nothing happens. Two, the needle turns. Three, the needle spins round and round, forever. Show me your fingers.

n403p.text: One. A compass needle always points North and South. Nothing can change that.

n404m.text: Two! I think the needle is a tiny magnet. Then Basil's magnet can attract it, or repel it.

n405b.text: Two! My magnet pulls and pushes other magnets. The needle will turn!

n501.text: Be the compass needle! Shrink down. Quietly.

n502.text: You are the needle inside a compass, balanced on a tiny pin. You can turn freely.

n503.text: You swing, and slow, and stop. Your red end points to the North.

n504.text: Here comes a bar magnet! Your red end is pushed away. The magnet turns round, and now your red end is pulled in.

n505.text: The magnet goes away. You swing back to the North-South direction.

n601.text: The answer is two: the needle turns towards or away from the magnet! Did you show two fingers? Put one finger up!

n602b.text: The needle is the small magnet inside a compass, such as this thin red one. My magnet attracted one end, and repelled the other!

n701b.text: Easy! The needle points to the letter N. If I turn the compass round, the needle turns round with it!

n702.text: Look closer. Turn the compass round. The letters turn, but the needle does not!

n703.text: So turn the compass until the N sits under the needle's red end. Now you know which way is North!

n704m.text: A compass is a tool that helps us find the direction, such as my hiking compass!

n707.text: A compass can help us to find the direction. When the needle inside the compass stops moving, it always points in the North-South direction of the Earth.

n801.text: Showdown! Double points. Momo's compass checklist has one mistake. Line one, two, or three? Show me with your fingers.

n802m.text: One: hold the compass flat, so the needle can turn freely. Two: wait until the needle stops moving. Three: keep Basil's magnet right next to the compass, to help it.

n804b.text: Three! My magnet attracts and repels the needle. Then the needle cannot show the North-South direction!

n805.text: Three fingers? Put up two more on your score hand! Keep magnets and phones away from your compass.

n901p.text: But what if it is night, and we cannot see the Sun? Will a compass still work?

n902.text: Look closer. At night, a ship sails in the Singapore Strait. Clouds hide the stars.

n903.text: But the needle in the ship's compass still comes to rest in the North-South direction.

n904.text: Far away in the United States, a hiker is lost in thick fog. Her compass works there too!

n905p.text: Tell the direction means find out which way is North, South, East or West, such as on a ship at night!

n907.text: Hence, a freely suspended magnet can be used to tell the direction.

c1003.text: Hang it freely? North-South! A compass needle? A small magnet! Why North-South? Earth behaves like a magnet!

n1101.text: Show me your score hand! Two fingers or more? You beat the Buddies. Three fingers? High five!

n1102.text: Did you spot the sea turtle? It was in the seagrass, at the end of the boardwalk!

n1103p.text: Here is a fun fact! Sea turtles can feel the Earth's magnet. It helps them find their way across the ocean, back to the beach where they hatched!

n1201.text: Next time: Pip strokes an iron nail with Basil's magnet, again and again, always the same way. Then he holds the nail near some steel paper clips. What happens? One, nothing happens. Two, the nail attracts the clips. Lock in your answer!

h860.text: Let's read today's key words together! Ready?
